title: Bram and the Portrait
premise: Folklorist Wren Quintana arrives in the mountain village of Salcedo to record a lullaby that locals refuse to sing twice, only to find the mirrors in their rented house lagging one second behind reality—and in that stolen second, something else is looking back. The lag traces to 1974, when Wren's grandmother, then the village's song-collector, took a portrait of the dead rather than returning it, binding the village's grief into glass. As the delay stretches from one second to ten, villagers begin vanishing into their own reflections, and Wren realizes the entity will not stop until what was taken is given back. In the end, Wren must choose between destroying the portrait and losing their own reflection forever—or surrendering their face to the glass so the village's dead can finally rest.
about_author: Lena Villalobos is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing funeral songs across rural Iberia before turning to horror. She writes in a farmhouse with every mirror covered, which she insists is for drafts, not protection.

chapters.title: The Song They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Wren arrives in Salcedo with recording equipment and professional skepticism, interviewing elderly residents about a lullaby no one will perform twice. Old Marta sings it once, then goes pale and refuses. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into unease as the village's polite evasions reveal a shared, unspoken fear.

chapters.title: The House on Calle Espejo
chapters.summary: Wren settles into a cheap rental on Mirror Street, noticing the landlady has removed every mirror except one sealed behind wallpaper. Wren peels it free that night. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery, tinged with the first real wrongness—the room feels watched even when empty.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Wren notices their reflection blinks after they do. Testing with a metronome, they confirm the mirror lags exactly one second. A neighbor, Tomás, sees the uncovered mirror through the window and warns them to cover it or leave. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: rationalist delight giving way to dread as the data refuses natural explanation.

chapters.title: What the Delay Contains
chapters.summary: In the lagging second, Wren glimpses the reflection moving independently—turning its head toward them. They film it; the footage shows nothing. Tomás reveals children here are taught never to look at mirrors at dusk. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: isolation deepens as evidence dissolves and belief becomes the only currency.

chapters.title: The Collector of 1974
chapters.summary: Digging through parish records, Wren finds their grandmother listed as a visiting song-collector in 1974—the same year eleven villagers died in a flood and were buried without rites. Among her archived effects: a crate shipped home, contents unknown. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: the horror of inheritance, realizing family history is the crime scene.

chapters.title: Marta's Confession
chapters.summary: Marta, dying and past fear, tells Wren the flood dead appeared in mirrors for weeks afterward, begging to be sung home. Wren's grandmother photographed the mirror instead of singing—capturing the dead in a portrait she kept. The lag began the day the portrait left. POV: Marta, framed within Wren's visit. Emotional beat: grief and fury braided together; the debt has a face now.

chapters.title: Ten Seconds
chapters.summary: The lag doubles overnight. Wren watches their reflection finish movements they haven't started, and once, smile without cause. The village holds a silent procession, covering windows with black cloth. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: loss of control—the phenomenon is accelerating, indifferent to Wren's schedule or sanity.

chapters.title: The Vanishing of Señora Ibáñez
chapters.summary: The landlady is found standing before her bathroom mirror, alive but absent-eyed, her reflection gone while she remains—a hollow woman repeating the lullaby's first line. The village blames Wren's arrival. POV: Tomás. Emotional beat: guilt made communal; Wren understands they brought the reckoning closer.

chapters.title: Letters Home
chapters.summary: Wren contacts their mother, learning the family crate from 1974 sits unopened in an attic in Oviedo. Shipping records show grandmother tried to return to Salcedo twice and turned back both times. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: dread of the journey ahead; the past literally waits in a box.

chapters.title: Into the Glass
chapters.summary: Señora Ibáñez walks into her mirror and does not come out. The village seals her house. That night Wren's reflection speaks their grandmother's name. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: terror crossing into compulsion—the entity isn't haunting Wren; it's recruiting them.

chapters.title: The Priest Who Keeps No Mirrors
chapters.summary: Father Anselmo, whose church has been mirrorless since 1974, gives Wren his account: the dead don't want worship, they want completion—an unfinished burial song cut off mid-verse by the flood. The portrait holds the verse's ending. POV: Father Anselmo. Emotional beat: reluctant hope; there may be a rite, not just a return.

chapters.title: The Attic in Oviedo
chapters.summary: Wren travels home and opens the crate: the portrait, wrapped in a funeral shroud, showing eleven faces pressed against the inside of painted glass. Their mother confesses grandmother heard it singing every night until her death. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: confrontation with the beloved dead; love and theft were the same act.

chapters.title: It Follows the Portrait
chapters.summary: Driving back, Wren checks a rest-stop restroom mirror: the lag is already there, waiting. The reflection mouths the missing verse. Wren understands distance was never protection—the portrait carries the boundary with it. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: claustrophobic inevitability; running was always impossible.

chapters.title: The Village Decides
chapters.summary: Wren returns to find Salcedo holding a tense assembly: some want the portrait burned, others believe destruction frees the dead into everyone's reflections. Tomás defends Wren publicly, splitting the village. POV: Tomás. Emotional beat: solidarity against fear; duty and mercy pull the town apart.

chapters.title: The Verse Recovered
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing grandmother's field notes with Anselmo's liturgy, Wren reconstructs the interrupted burial song—but the final line exists only inside the portrait, sung by the trapped dead themselves. Someone must listen from within reach of the glass. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: grim clarity; the solution requires proximity to the trap.

chapters.title: First Attempt: Fire
chapters.summary: A faction burns the portrait's frame in the square. The canvas won't catch; instead every mirror in Salcedo lags simultaneously, and three more villagers go reflection-silent. Wren is blamed openly now. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: despair and rage—half-measures make it worse, and time has nearly run out.

chapters.title: The Price Named
chapters.summary: Anselmo reveals the rite's cost: the singer must stand where the collector stood and offer what she withheld—not just the portrait, but a living reflection to anchor the dead's passage home. One face, freely given, stays behind in the glass. POV: Father Anselmo. Emotional beat: the theme crystallizes—survival has always been someone else's price.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Tomás, who has grown close to Wren, tries to take their place, arguing he belongs to the village and its debt. Wren refuses: the theft was their blood's, and the entity answers only to the collector's line. A bitter, tender standoff. POV: alternating Wren and Tomás. Emotional beat: love refusing to be sacrificed to duty, and duty refusing to be dodged.

chapters.title: The Night of the Long Second
chapters.summary: The lag reaches a full minute; the whole village moves through a world slightly behind itself. The dead appear in every window, singing the verse up to its final line, waiting. Wren carries the portrait to the flooded chapel ruins where grandmother first failed them. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: apocalyptic stillness—the world holding its breath.

chapters.title: Returning What Was Taken
chapters.summary: In the ruins, Wren sings the completed verse before the portrait and offers their reflection. The glass opens like water; the eleven dead step through their own painted faces and dissolve into song. Wren's reflection remains behind, smiling, taking their place. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: catharsis and grief entwined—the debt paid, but paid in flesh.

chapters.title: The Face Left Behind
chapters.summary: Wren wakes reflected nowhere: shop windows, spoons, dark screens all pass them through. The village mirrors run true again. Tomás stays anyway, saying you can love someone the glass doesn't hold. POV: Tomás. Emotional beat: quiet devastation softened by chosen companionship; survival redefined as what remains, not what's kept.

chapters.title: Coda: The Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Months later, Wren records Marta's lullaby at last—and sings it back to the village, twice, to weeping applause. On Mirror Street, in the one uncovered mirror, a familiar silhouette lingers a half-second after Wren passes, watching kindly. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: bittersweet closure—the price paid echoes forever, but the song is whole.
